1.title: Governance and Compliance
1.text: Welcome to Module 10. This is the first of three Business Environment modules, and the Business Environment domain carries twenty-six percent of the exam. This module covers two tasks that frame everything else. Governance is how decisions are made and who makes them. And compliance is the set of rules the project is bound by. Part 1 covers governance. Part 2 covers compliance.

1.title: Where This Module Sits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits. The Business Environment domain has eight tasks, and this module covers two. Task one: define and establish governance. That includes structure, rules, procedures and reporting. It includes ethics and policies, success metrics, and escalation paths and thresholds. Task two: plan and manage compliance, from confirming requirements to measuring how compliant the project is. A reliable exam habit: when a decision exceeds your authority and no threshold exists, work with the sponsor to define it. Do not infer it.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Explain organizational versus project governance, and right-size it. Choose between structured governance and self-governance. Establish structure, rules, reporting, ethics and policies from process assets. Define success metrics, escalation paths and thresholds. Confirm, classify and plan compliance, and analyze threats and consequences. And use methods to support compliance and measure how compliant the project is.

1.title: Case Check-In: Governance of the Microgrid
1.text: Our microgrid has hybrid governance. A steering committee, chaired by the Provost's office, oversees funding discipline and milestones. A change control board decides baseline changes above your threshold. The product owner, Priya Nair, orders the backlog for the software lane. You are the project manager, integrating all of it. Thresholds on cost, schedule, scope, quality and reserve use are agreed with the sponsor. None is assumed from the past.

1.title: What Project Governance Is
1.text: Project governance is the framework, functions and processes that guide project management decisions and activities to optimize value delivery. It is holistic and integrative, considering all other performance domains. It ensures alignment with the portfolio, strategy and goals. It often uses technology and data for real-time tracking and reporting. It includes the authority to cancel a project when necessary. And it is shaped by the performing organization's governance model, and by stakeholders such as customers and regulators. Right-size it: focus on value delivery, not bureaucracy.

1.title: Organizational and Project Governance
1.text: Organizational governance gives direction and control for the whole organization through policies, processes, procedures and decisions. It is overseen by executives, and aims at transparency, oversight, compliance, resilience and alignment of portfolios, programs and projects with strategy. Project governance applies specific processes and frameworks to manage individual projects effectively. It is overseen by the sponsor, a steering committee or board, the PMO, the project manager, or the team in self-governance. Too much governance wastes resources. Too little causes misalignment.

1.title: What Governance Decides
1.text: The Governance domain makes ten kinds of choices. Establish a governance framework aligned with strategy and ethics. Define roles and responsibilities for decision-making, oversight and control. Ensure communication and coordination. Monitor and manage dependencies, risks, issues and escalations. Continuously assess and improve the framework. Balance competing demands. Tailor processes to objectives. Manage interdependencies among domains. Build in feedback mechanisms. And ensure compliance with regulatory and legal requirements.

1.title: Governance Scenarios
1.text: PMBOK 8 describes five governance scenarios. Project initiation: a venture is deemed worthwhile. Project replanning: revising any plan element that needs deliberate review. Project expansion or contraction: changing constraints to preserve or capture value. Early termination for positive cause: the desired value was achieved before the schedule or budget was used up. Early termination for negative cause: the desired value is no longer achievable. In each, the overarching value proposition is the primary factor.

1.title: Governance Models
1.text: Two models. Structured governance often has an executive sponsor, a PMO leader, some governance board and a project manager. It suits predictive, large, regulated work, with mechanisms such as a board, change control board, phase gates and formal reporting. Its challenge is bureaucracy and slow decisions. Guided self-governance suits adaptive work: the team decides within guardrails, using reviews, retrospectives and team agreements. Its challenge is fragmented decisions, fixed with clear measurable common objectives, leading indicators and feedback. Hybrid projects use a moderate or combined model.

1.title: Establish Governance From Process Assets
1.text: Governance is not invented from scratch. It draws on organizational process assets and environmental factors, and the result is recorded in the project management plan or a governance plan. The PMO, where one exists, often establishes the governance policies, processes and templates, may lead structured governance, and reviews and approves tailoring. Organizational policies are not updated by the project. They are tailored within policy. Also identify the control boards, committees and stakeholders involved, and decide whether the team will have its own governance board.

1.title: Elements of a Governance Framework
1.text: Five elements make up the framework. Structure: who sponsors, steers and decides. That includes the sponsor, board, change control board and PMO. It includes roles, a responsibility matrix, and decision rights. Rules and procedures: the life cycle and phase gates, change control, issue and defect management, work authorization, verification, validation and closure requirements. Policies: compliance, security, procurement, data protection, sustainability and AI use. Reporting: requirements, formats, cadence and dashboards. Ethics: the code of conduct, conflict-of-interest disclosure and fairness. All are recorded in the plan.

1.title: Define Success Metrics
1.text: Effective governance needs three components. Target metrics clearly aligned with strategic goals. Signaling mechanisms, or alarm systems, typically leading indicators that show whether delivery is moving toward the goal. And feedback mechanisms, so decision-makers learn and improve. Examples: the effectiveness of prioritization decisions, due-date performance, and whether the current integrated baseline carries the highest value proposition. Prefer outcome measures to input metrics. Make metrics specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound, with tolerance thresholds that trigger action.

1.title: Metrics Governance Tracks
1.text: Governance tracks several kinds of metric. Leading indicators reveal upcoming trends: backlog items in progress, a missing risk process, unengaged stakeholders and poorly defined success criteria. Lagging indicators measure after the fact: deliverables completed, variances and resources consumed. Governance also tracks, regularly, status and progress, and resource needs. It tracks risks and escalation criteria, and benefits realized. And it tracks change control, compliance, issues and funding. Success has two dimensions: project management success and outcome success. Watch the measurement pitfalls from Module 6.

1.title: Escalation Paths and Thresholds
1.text: Define the path and the thresholds early: who decides what, up to what limit, and to whom a matter goes next. The team decides within agreed guardrails. The project manager decides up to a stated limit. Matters above that go to the sponsor, and the largest to the steering committee. When a decision is beyond the team's authority, the team investigates alternatives, considers the impact of each, and escalates to the person with proper authority. That is the idea behind the saying: do not bring me problems, bring me solutions. Do not infer authority from past decisions.

1.title: No Threshold Defined
1.text: Here is a common exam pattern. A decision exceeds your spending authority, and no threshold exists. The wrong answers are to take the decision yourself, to infer a limit from past projects, or to wait until it causes a problem. The right answer is to investigate alternatives and impacts, work with the sponsor to define the threshold, then follow it and record it. Unclear decision rights cause delay, so clarify them in the governance structure, for example with a responsibility matrix, not by assumption.

1.title: Escalation and Investment Control
1.text: Predictive environments add two governance components. Escalation is useful in hierarchical organizations where decision authority sits outside the team, or where higher-ranking people can remove persistent obstacles or resolve conflicts. Investment control applies where formal stewardship of funding is required, such as public corporations, government agencies and certain financial entities. It includes thorough risk evaluation, and decision points that decide whether the next round of funding still makes sense. Risks beyond your authority are escalated, and the receiving party must accept ownership.

1.title: Case Check-In: Escalating a Permit Delay
1.text: Suppose permit approval slips and the delay exceeds your authority. You investigate alternatives and the impact of each, and escalate to Elena Vasquez with a recommendation. The thresholds agreed earlier, for example a schedule slip beyond two weeks or cost beyond two percent of the budget, tell you when to escalate. Report the slip early and factually. Keeping status honest makes escalation timely. The decision is recorded and communicated.

1.title: Sourcing and Tailoring Governance
1.text: Sourcing strategy is a governance decision, with effects on schedule, scope, finance, resource capacity and risk. Insourcing suits culture, differentiating skills and proximity, and outsourcing suits specialized skills and scaled or variable capacity. Tailor governance to the industry, regulation, organization and project context. Customizing governance is typically part of Initiate Project or Phase, and may be iterative. A small project's manager decides with key leaders. A project needing rapid innovation may use self-governance with no external body. A multinational project integrates governance across domains and handles regional variation at program or portfolio level.

1.title: Governance in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
1.text: Governance differs by approach. Predictive: a structured model with a sponsor, PMO, board and project manager. Decisions at gates and through the change control board. A formal escalation path with thresholds. And status reports and dashboards. The risk is over-control. Agile: guided self-governance, with decisions in reviews and retrospectives and by the product owner, impediments escalated to the facilitator and sponsor, and reporting through radiators and burn charts. The risk is fragmented decisions. Hybrid: a combined model, with one consolidated view for governance, and a clear answer to who decides what.

1.title: Governance Traps: What PMI Expects
1.text: The traps for governance. Define escalation paths and thresholds, and do not infer them. Unclear decision rights cause delay, so clarify them in the structure, not by assumption. Right-size governance, and give self-governance guardrails. Follow the structure, including customer governance requirements and audits, and do not bypass the change control board or the steering committee. Use outcome metrics and leading indicators, and keep reports honest. Governance has authority to stop a project. And ethics and feedback are part of governance.

1.title: Part 1 Recap
1.text: Let us recap Part 1. Governance is a framework for decisions that optimize value delivery, and it can cancel a project. The models are structured, guided self-governance and hybrid. The framework has structure, rules, policies, reporting and ethics, drawn from process assets. Metrics have target, signaling and feedback components, and favor leading and outcome measures. Define escalation paths and thresholds early, with the sponsor. And right-size governance, remembering that sourcing is a governance decision. In Part 2, we turn to compliance.

2.title: Compliance: Key Terms
2.text: Part 2 covers compliance. Key terms. Compliance means meeting the requirements the project is bound by: laws and regulations, standards, contractual terms and organizational policies. A regulation is a requirement imposed by a governmental body. A compliance requirement is a specific obligation: a rule, control, report, certification, approval, test or record. Mandatory requirements come from law, regulation or contract, and voluntary ones are optional standards adopted by decision. A threat to compliance is a risk until it occurs, then an issue. Compliance evidence is the records that prove it.

2.title: Where Compliance Requirements Come From
2.text: Compliance requirements come from seven kinds of source. Legal restrictions: laws on security, data protection, business conduct, employment and procurement. Government and industry standards: for environment, safety, quality and workmanship. Public health and safety regulations. Other factors, such as taxes, tariffs, geopolitical limits and emerging-technology rules. Organizational policies and procedures. Contracts and agreements: customer and supplier terms, service-level agreements and flow-down clauses. And stakeholder commitments, such as sustainability indicators and stricter customer standards. A project may even be terminated for compliance reasons.

2.title: Confirm Compliance Requirements
2.text: Confirm compliance requirements in five steps. Identify what applies by jurisdiction, industry, product, data type, technology, location and market. Consult the experts: legal and compliance, subject matter experts, regulators and certifying bodies, and review contracts and policies. Confirm with the sponsor and governance which obligations are mandatory, which are voluntary, and who is accountable. Record them where work is planned: requirements, quality requirements, the WBS or backlog, the schedule, the budget and the assumption log. Do it early, and reconfirm when scope, location, supplier or technology changes.

2.title: Classify Compliance Categories
2.text: Classify requirements into categories, because each has different owners, experts, evidence and risk. The categories are a study aid. Legal and regulatory, with permits and licenses. Security and privacy, with tests and access logs. Health and safety, with inspections and plans. Environmental and sustainability, with measurements and certifications. Quality and industry standards. Financial and reporting. Contractual, with compliance matrices. And organizational policy and ethics. Classification also separates mandatory from voluntary and sets priority by consequence and deadline.

2.title: Examples of Fast-Changing Situations
2.text: Some situations change fast. A regulation takes effect in three months: confirm its requirements and prioritize them in the backlog. Data about children or health: check residency and privacy obligations before choosing storage. A restricted ingredient in one export market: determine the compliance approach before launch. A new substance: determine which regulations apply, with experts. A rule changes in mid-project: reassess scope and backlog, and reprioritize by effective date and consequence. In every case, releasing first and fixing later breaks the rule.

2.title: Threats to Compliance
2.text: Threats to compliance come from changes in rules and changes in the project. They come from third parties, and gaps in knowledge and behavior. And they come from missing evidence, technology, jurisdictional differences and timing. Examples include a supplier that does not meet requirements, and staff without certification. They include data processing abroad, and uncontrolled files. And they include an unvetted AI tool processing personal data, or permit delays. Treat threats as risks: register them with an owner and a response. When a threat occurs, it becomes an issue: log it, run the planned response, update the register and inform stakeholders. Insurance transfers loss, but does not create compliance.

2.title: Consequences of Noncompliance
2.text: Analyze the consequences of noncompliance, as a grouping from exam practice. Harm to people or the environment. Stop-work orders or loss of license to operate. Fines, penalties and legal action. Contract termination or penalties. Rework and delay, because fixing later costs more. Loss of market access and reputation. Assess likelihood and impact, and who is affected. Compare the cost of compliance with the cost of noncompliance. For mandatory requirements, the question is how, not whether. Document the analysis, and show it to the sponsor and governance.

2.title: Deadline Against a Mandatory Requirement
2.text: Suppose a deadline conflicts with a mandatory requirement. Mandatory means comply. Present the consequences and schedule-safe alternatives to the sponsor and governance. If a shortcut would bypass an internal policy, it needs a formal exception through governance, with risk analysis. It must not be a private decision, and there are no silent workarounds. Free improvements still go through change control. And document the analysis, because it supports decisions, audits and escalation.

2.title: Determine the Compliance Approach
2.text: Choose the approach by situation. A mandatory requirement: build it in. Add it to scope, the WBS or backlog, the schedule and the budget. Add it to the definition of done or phase exit criteria. Assign an owner, plan how compliance will be verified, train, and monitor. A voluntary standard: evaluate value, cost and risk with governance, then adopt it or document a formal exception. A known threat: a risk response. Supplier obligations: put them in the contract, with evidence and audit rights. A rule change: reassess scope and backlog, reprioritize and raise change requests.

2.title: Methods That Support Compliance
2.text: Many methods support compliance. Governance and policies define standards and thresholds. A compliance matrix maps each requirement to an owner, control, verification method, evidence and status. Requirements traceability links requirements to deliverables, tests and acceptance. The definition of done and acceptance criteria put checks into each iteration. Checklists confirm obligations at gates. Audits and inspections test against standards. Training builds awareness. Controls and approvals segregate duties. A controlled repository keeps approved versions findable. Supplier clauses and audits flow requirements down. When a regulator requires a reporting format, standardize inputs at the source.

2.title: Compliance Matrix and Statuses
2.text: A compliance matrix records, for each requirement, an owner, a control, a verification method, evidence and a status. It ties to the requirements traceability matrix. Compliant means the control is in place and evidence is available. Partially compliant means the control covers only part of the scope, for example a retention rule enforced in some systems but not others. Non-compliant means no control or no evidence. Not applicable means the requirement does not apply to the project. This is exam practice. The example shows four requirements with different statuses.

2.title: Measure Compliance
2.text: Measure the extent to which the project is compliant. PMBOK 8 points to compliance audits or checklists against standards and benchmarks, metrics that track compliance with policies, and verification at closure that all obligations were met. As exam practice, track the share of requirements implemented and verified, and open audit findings by number, severity and age. Track nonconformances, and permits and certifications obtained against due. Track training completion, incidents and breaches, and the supplier compliance rate. Add sustainability indicators and compliance cost against plan. Report with a dashboard and escalate what threatens a mandatory requirement.

2.title: Case Check-In: Compliance on the Microgrid
2.text: On the microgrid, compliance spans four areas. The Planning and Permits Office and the utility approve permits and the grid interconnection, tracked as external milestones. Data about campus users on the dashboard is stored under privacy rules chosen before design. Battery and electrical safety inspections are built into phase exit criteria. Emissions and construction noise are measured against commitments to Eastgate residents. Each has an owner, a control and evidence, in a compliance matrix kept in a controlled repository.

2.title: Supplier Compliance and Multinational Work
2.text: Supplier compliance is yours to enforce. Put requirements in the contract, require evidence and audit rights, and enforce them. Stop affected work until a noncompliant supplier meets the requirement. Multinational projects must follow different regional rules, so coordinate variations through program or portfolio governance. Do not ignore the human side. Training and a speak-up culture are compliance controls. And adoption suffers when compliance feels like a tax, so connect it to value people care about. And verify obligations at closure before closing the project.

2.title: Compliance in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
2.text: Compliance differs by approach. Predictive: requirements up front in the documentation and traceability matrix. Verification through phase exit criteria, gate reviews and audits. A controlled repository. And change control with compliance review. Agile: compliance items go into the backlog, prioritized by effective date and consequence, and new rules reprioritize it. The definition of done includes compliance checks every iteration, and evidence is lightweight but traceable. Hybrid: fixed regulatory requirements in the baseline, others in the backlog, gates for regulated parts.

2.title: Compliance Traps: What PMI Expects
2.text: The traps for compliance. A compliance requirement is a requirement: confirm it, plan it, verify it and evidence it. Do not borrow rules from a different situation: a new product, market or data type needs fresh confirmation. Classify requirements, assign owners, and plan the verification method. Put compliance in the definition of done or exit criteria, not in a final audit. Threats are risks, and insurance does not create compliance. Mandatory means comply, and exceptions go through governance. A new rule reshapes the backlog or scope.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap the whole module. Governance: a right-sized framework from process assets, with escalation and thresholds defined with the sponsor. Models: structured, self-governing with guardrails, or combined. Compliance: confirm requirements early, classify them, assign owners and plan the verification. Threats are risks until they occur, and the consequences go to the sponsor. Methods: put compliance in the definition of done, keep a compliance matrix, audit, and keep evidence in a controlled repository. Now it is time to test yourself. Five questions follow. For each one, pause the video, choose your answer, and then listen to the explanation.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A decision on a vendor change order exceeds the project manager's spending authority, and no threshold exists for it. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. Authority is defined, not inferred, so the project manager investigates alternatives and works with the sponsor to define the threshold. Inferring authority from the past, waiting for a claim, or splitting the order each avoid the governance decision.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A self-governing agile team makes decisions that often contradict one another, and stakeholders are confused about priorities. What would help most? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. Fragmented decision-making in self-governance is fixed by shared measurable objectives, leading indicators and feedback mechanisms inside clear guardrails. Heavy approvals, an appointed dictator, or stopping records remove the guardrails or the transparency.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. An optional industry accessibility standard would add three weeks to the plan, and the contract does not require it. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Voluntary standards are evaluated for value, cost and risk with governance, which then either adopts them or records a formal, documented exception. Skipping silently, waiting for a complaint, or adopting without approval each avoid that decision.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A mandatory data-protection rule will take effect in three months, and the team has no work planned for it. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. A new mandatory rule is confirmed early and reshapes the backlog by effective date and consequence, with an owner and a plan to verify compliance. Waiting, treating it as voluntary, or a general statement do not plan the work.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Auditors ask an agile team to show that each regulatory requirement is implemented and verified, but the requirements are scattered across several documents. What would best support the team? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. A compliance matrix ties each requirement to an owner, control, verification method and evidence, and links to traceability. Narratives, promises, or a final audit do not give measurable, current evidence.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: C. With no threshold, work with the sponsor to define one. Question two: A. Self-governance needs shared objectives, leading indicators and feedback. Question three: D. Weigh a voluntary standard with governance, then adopt or document an exception. Question four: B. Confirm a new mandatory rule early and prioritize it in the backlog. Question five: A. A compliance matrix links each requirement to controls and evidence. That completes Module 10. Next, Module 11 covers risk management, issues and impediments. See you there.
